What's the difference between a custom-tiled shower and an acrylic system?

A custom-tiled shower gives you full control over size, shape, tile and finish — it is the right call when you want the bathroom to be a feature. An acrylic or composite wall system is quicker to install and lower maintenance, with a non-porous surface that resists mold and mildew. We will price both so you can compare honestly.
How does the two-day tub-to-shower conversion work?

We pull the old tub or surround, prep the space, and install the new low-entry base and wall system — typically over about two days with virtually no dust or mess. It is the option most people choose when they want the bathroom back quickly without weeks of construction.
What keeps a custom tile shower from leaking down the line?

Waterproof membranes, a properly sloped pan and careful substrate prep before a single tile goes up. Those three things direct water where it should go and protect the framing behind the walls — and they are exactly where a cheap bid usually cuts corners.

How is the floor drain handled on a curbless pan?

Custom Tiled Shower vs. Acrylic System — Which One Is Actually Right For You?
The honest trade-offs between a fully tiled custom shower and a two-day acrylic wall system, from a contractor who installs both.

This is the first real decision in almost every bathroom project we quote, and it gets decided badly more often than any other. People pick tile because it photographs well, or acrylic because it is cheaper, and neither of those is the actual question.

## What a custom tiled shower buys you

Design freedom, mostly. A tiled shower can be any size, any shape, any slope. It can wrap a corner, run to the ceiling, take a bench along one wall and a niche exactly where your shampoo bottles actually go. Nothing about it is constrained to the sizes a factory decided to mold.

It also holds value differently. Large-format porcelain, a mosaic pan and frameless glass read as a deliberate choice to anyone walking through the house — including a buyer.

The cost is time and dependency on workmanship. A tiled shower is built in stages: substrate, waterproof membrane, sloped pan, tile, grout, seal. Each of those has to cure or set before the next one starts. And every one of those stages is a place where a contractor in a hurry can cut something you will not be able to see until it fails.

## What an acrylic or composite system buys you

Speed and predictability. The walls arrive as engineered panels, they go up over a properly prepped substrate, and the whole conversion is usually finished in about two days. There is no tile layout to get wrong and no grout to seal.

Maintenance is genuinely easier. A non-porous surface has nowhere for soap scum and mildew to take hold, so cleaning is a wipe rather than a scrub and a grout brush.

The trade-off is that you are choosing from a catalog. Sizes, patterns and finishes are what the manufacturer makes. If your space is unusual, or you want something specific, tile is the only way to get there.

## How to actually choose

Ask yourself three questions in this order:

**Is this bathroom the feature, or the utility?** A master bath you will look at every day for twenty years justifies tile. A rental turnover, a guest bath or a hall bathroom that just needs to work usually does not.

**How long can the room be out of service?** If it is the only full bath in the house, two days versus two weeks is not a preference, it is the whole decision.

**Is the space standard or awkward?** A sloped ceiling, an odd corner, a curbless entry or a footprint the factory sizes do not fit — that is tile territory by default.

## The one thing that matters either way

Whatever goes on the wall, the waterproofing behind it decides whether the shower lasts. Membrane, slope and substrate prep are not optional on either system, and they are the least visible part of the invoice. If a bid comes in dramatically under everyone else's, that gap came from somewhere — and this is almost always where.

I have personally torn out and rebuilt dozens of showers that failed for exactly that reason. Tile or acrylic, the part you cannot see is the part you are actually paying for.

Designing A Walk-In Shower For Aging In Place (Without It Looking Like A Hospital)
Low-entry pans, real grab-bar blocking, bench seats and fixture placement — the accessibility decisions that have to be made before the walls close up.

We do a lot of this work around Indian Land and Sun City, and the request nearly always arrives the same way: someone has had a scare, or is planning ahead after watching a parent struggle, and they want the bathroom to stop being the most dangerous room in the house.

The good news is that nearly every accessibility decision also happens to make a shower nicer to use. The catch is that most of them have to be made before framing closes up.

## Get rid of the step-over

A tub edge is the actual hazard. Climbing over a fourteen-inch wall of wet acrylic, on a wet floor, is where people fall.

A low-entry pan drops that to an inch or two. A curbless pan removes it entirely, but it needs the floor structure to allow the drain and slope — which is exactly the kind of thing to establish at the consultation rather than mid-demo.

## Grab bars need blocking, not anchors

This is the one that matters most and gets skipped most.

A grab bar screwed into drywall with toggle anchors will hold a towel. It will not reliably hold a falling adult, which is the entire point of it. Proper installation means plywood blocking fixed between the studs, put in while the wall is open, so the bar is anchored into structure.

If the walls are already closed, you are choosing between opening them again or accepting a bar you cannot trust. Decide before demo.

And they no longer have to look institutional — matte black, brushed nickel and brass finishes are all readily available, and they read as fixtures rather than medical equipment.

## Sit down and check the reach

A built-in bench is the difference between a shower someone can use independently and one they need help with. Tile it into the wall rather than adding a folding seat later, and it becomes part of the design instead of an accessory.

Then place the fixtures for someone sitting on it. A handheld on a slide bar you can reach seated, and a valve you can operate from the bench rather than only from the doorway. This is a five-minute conversation at design stage that changes the entire experience of the room.

## The floor is the last thing people think about

Big glossy tile on a shower pan looks superb and is exactly the wrong choice underfoot when wet. Small-format mosaic gives you far more grout line per square foot, and grout lines are grip. A pebble or hex pan is both the safer option and, in most bathrooms, the better-looking one.

## Do it now, not later

The reason to build this into a remodel you were doing anyway is simple economics. Blocking, a curbless pan and a tiled bench cost very little when the walls are already open. Retrofitting them into a finished bathroom means tearing out work you just paid for.

If accessibility is anywhere on your list — even five or ten years out — say so at the consultation. It costs almost nothing to build in and a great deal to add on.

What Actually Drives The Price Of A Bathroom Remodel
The variables that move a bathroom quote up or down, and why the cheapest bid is so often the most expensive job.

Nobody publishes a price for a bathroom because nobody honestly can. What I can do is tell you exactly which levers move the number, so you can walk into a consultation knowing where your money is going.

## The variables that matter most

**Whether plumbing moves.** This is the single biggest swing. Keeping the drain and valve where they are is straightforward. Moving a drain across a joist bay, or relocating a valve to a different wall, means opening the floor or wall and getting it inspected. It is not exotic work, but it is real work.

**Pan style.** A pre-formed base drops in. A fully tiled pan is built by hand — mud bed, slope, membrane, then mosaic — and takes days rather than hours. Both are correct choices; they just are not the same price.

**Tile size and material.** Large-format porcelain needs a flatter substrate than small tile, so the prep work goes up before a single piece is set. Natural stone needs sealing and different handling than porcelain. Mosaic pans take far longer to lay than a sheet base.

**Glass.** A fixed panel is one price. A frameless enclosure with a hinged door and custom-cut glass is a different one, and it is usually the line item that surprises people most.

**Scope creep from what we find.** Behind a thirty-year-old surround there is sometimes rot, sometimes a hidden leak, sometimes framing that was never right. A good quote flags that risk before demo rather than discovering it and handing you a change order.

## Why the cheapest bid is usually the most expensive job

I am blunt about this because I have made a real part of my living fixing it.

The cheapest price almost never has value. It has to come from somewhere, and it does not come from a contractor deciding to earn less — it comes out of waterproofing, out of substrate prep, out of the time it takes to set tile properly. Those are the parts you cannot inspect once the job is finished, which is precisely why they are where corners get cut. When it fails in three years, you pay twice: once for the tear-out, once for the rebuild.

The other end is not automatically value either. A very high number often just means a large company subbing the work out to a crew you will never meet, with the margin paying for the office rather than the craftsmanship.

The middle ground is generally where price and value actually meet. That is where we sit, deliberately.

## What to ask any contractor you are considering

- What waterproofing system are you using, and does it go behind the whole wet wall?
- Who is physically on my job every day — you, an employee, or a sub?
- Is the tile you are proposing rated for a wet space?
- What happens to the schedule and the price if you open the wall and find rot?
- Can I see a shower you built five years ago, not just five weeks ago?

The answers will tell you more than the number at the bottom of the page.
